summary.text: A male neonate was delivered by cesarean section at an estimated 38 weeks after prenatal ultrasound showed long-bone shortening and bowing, thoracic hypoplasia and contractures, with fetal growth restriction. Apgar scores were 3, 3, 6 and 9, birth weight was 3440 g, and examination showed dysmorphic features, a hypoplastic chest and abnormal finger and toe positioning. He received non-invasive ventilation, was transferred to the NICU and was intubated at 5 h of life for worsening respiratory distress.

Serial echocardiograms confirmed severe suprasystemic PPHN with right-to-left shunting and right ventricular pressure overload, and the oxygenation index reached 48 on day 3. Support was escalated with HFOV, iNO 25 ppm and catecholamines; ECMO criteria were met but extracorporeal support was not initiated because of instability. Workup found a structurally normal heart and negative blood cultures, and whole-exome sequencing identified two pathogenic LIFR nonsense variants in trans, establishing Stüve–Wiedemann syndrome.

Oxygenation improved from day 5, iNO was discontinued on day 8, pupillary reactivity returned on day 10 and catecholamines were weaned from day 11. Ventilation moved to PRVC on day 13 and NAVA with FiO_(2) 0.21 from day 14, and echocardiography on day 14 showed a closed ductus and normal septal kinetics. Inflammatory markers rose and fell with antibiotic changes, and a central line culture grew Enterobacter hormaechei.

The admission was complicated by recurrent hyperthermia up to 41.5 °C with tachycardia and agitation, severe hypoxic–ischemic brain injury on MRI, and seizures confirmed on aEEG on day 70 that were treated with phenobarbital and levetiracetam. A PEG tube was placed on day 56 and a tracheostomy on day 65. The infant was ultimately discharged under palliative home care in the third month of life.
